verdicts.note: Accurate and neutral. By the dramatic date (416 BC) Alcibiades was a leading Athenian politician and had already served as general (Thucydides has him general in 419 BC). He was famous in both roles by the narrator's time. The phrase only identifies him: no motive, judgment or argument is added, and 'famous' is neutral where 'notorious' would not be. It is his first gloss anywhere (1.0 names him bare), placed at his entrance. By ear, 'ringing through the courtyard' still attaches clearly to 'the voice'.
'Greetings' is current English for Jowett's 'Hail' (Plato: chairete). It keeps the mock-ceremonious tone of the garlanded entrance and pairs with the same salute at 8.8.

Jowett's 'contrived' is Alcibiades' jealous charge that Socrates engineered the seat (Plato: diemechanaso). 'Schemed to get a place' restores the accusation that 'managed to find' had lost, and it reads naturally.

Follows the glossary (fair, of persons = beautiful) and Plato's 'the most beautiful of those inside'. It matches 8.26 and 8.45. One side effect: 8.0 still calls the same man 'the handsomest' for Jowett's 'fairest' (see paragraph_problems).
Follows the glossary for Jowett's 'any other fair one' (Plato: kaloi oud' heni). It reads naturally, and 'them' still works after 'anyone'.

Accurate and consistent with the book's own chronology. 1.34 already says the victory came 'the day before yesterday, in the theater', before thirty thousand Greeks. 1.5, 1.13 and 1.36 put the victory sacrifice and party 'yesterday', the event Alcibiades says at 8.0 that he missed. Plato's proien at 213e is the same 'day before yesterday' as at 175e. Two words remove the clash without adding a fact, and the sentence still reads naturally.

Checked clause by clause against Jowett; nothing is dropped. The paragraph keeps the intolerable sobriety, the agreement on which he was let in, the self-appointed master, the goblet, the vessel of more than two quarts filled, drained and refilled for Socrates, the trick being useless on Socrates, and Socrates drinking. 'That can't be allowed' and 'master of the drinking' are, if anything, closer to Plato (ouk epitrepteon; archonta tes poseos). 'Drained' is right for 'emptied', since he drank it off (ekpiein). 'Wine-cooling bowl' avoids the modern bottled-drink sense. 'Well and truly drunk' stays within Jowett's 'well drunk'. The voice stays drunk, candid and funny ('that can't be allowed', 'let in', 'not one bit nearer'), and the quotes are balanced.
Drops the archaic 'Hail' and 'sire' but keeps the mock-grand salute, which dodges Eryximachus's complaint. 'The same to you' at 8.9 still answers it.

Right in direction. The directions are now easy to picture, the right-hand rule is clear for 8.43, and the contrast between not speaking and drinking your fill survives. But 'we had agreed' flattens Eryximachus's pompous officialese. 'Passed a resolution' renders Plato's decree formula (edoxen hemin); it is not archaic, and it was not among BL2's stated obstacles, which were 'spoken / well drunken' and the directions. It also echoes chapter 1, where his plan is a 'proposal' that Socrates calls a 'motion' no one will 'vote against' (1.43-1.47). Restore it and keep the rest of the edit.
verdicts.proposed_replace: 'Well,' said Eryximachus, 'before you arrived we had passed a resolution that each of us in turn, going round from left to right, should make a speech in praise of love, the best he could. All of us have spoken; you have not spoken, but you have drunk your fill, so you ought to speak. Then you can set Socrates any task you like, and he can set one for his neighbor on the right, and so on.'

verdicts.note: 'My dear friend' fits the ironic, affectionate vocative (Plato: o makarie). It matches 8.30 (same Greek, same fix) and 6.9.
Closer than 'For shame' to Plato's ouk euphemeseis ('hush, mind your words'), and still a reproach for what Alcibiades just claimed. It sets up the comic reversal 'Be quiet' at 8.16.

Keeps the oath and the point: while Socrates is present, no one else will be praised. Dropping 'for' leaves the reason implicit, but the juxtaposition makes it clear. The line is still brusque and drunk.
An exact modern equivalent.
'Urge' matches 'exhort' (Plato: keleuo). The 'not only ...; ...' construction reads naturally aloud.
Plato has o andres ('gentlemen'). 'My friends' matches Alcibiades' address at 8.6 and 8.38 and avoids the schoolmasterly ring.
Accurate: in legend Olympus is a musician and the pupil of Marsyas. The gloss comes before the name, so a listener never hears 'Olympus' as the gods' mountain.
Accurate: Pericles was the great Athenian statesman and orator. Minor: 8.37 now repeats 'the statesman Pericles'. This is harmless; trimming the gloss at 8.37 is optional (see paragraph_problems).

Right in direction, and faithful. Nothing is dropped, the register is now plain and heartfelt, and 'argue with' is apt for 'answer' (antilegein). Two unforced changes need fixing. (1) 'Admitted' breaks the link with 8.24, which still says 'he makes me confess'. Plato uses the same verb both times (homologein ... ta homologemena), Jowett keeps 'confess ... confessed', and 'confessed' is not archaic. (2) 'Wits' end' now clashes with 'wit's end' in 8.31, the same phrase in the same speech. The proposal uses Jowett's 'wit's end' to match 8.31; the alternative is to change 8.31 to 'wits' end' as well.
verdicts.proposed_replace: 'And he is the only person who has ever made me feel ashamed — which you might think was not in my nature — and no one else does. For I know that I cannot argue with him or say that I should not do what he tells me; but when I leave him, my love of popularity gets the better of me. So I run away from him and escape, and when I see him I am ashamed of what I have confessed to him. Many times I have wished he were dead, and yet I know that if he died I would be much more sorry than glad; so I am at my wit's end.

verdicts.note: Follows the glossary for Jowett's 'fair youth', and sharpens the irony against 8.26 ('drawn to beautiful young men').

Jowett's 'lovers whom I have ever had' means erastai (Plato: erastes), the men who courted him. 'Admirers' euphemized the role, and a bare 'lovers I have had' would now suggest past sexual partners. 'Lovers who have ever courted me' is frank and exact, follows the glossary's convention that the lover courts, and is picked up by 8.38's 'courting them ... court him'.
Jowett's comparison is generic ('a father or an elder brother'), and Plato has no possessive either.
The same vocative as 8.14 (o makarie), now rendered the same way. The nested-quote structure is unaffected.
Jowett's 'messed together' means they were messmates. The new wording makes clear that the two of them shared a mess, not that the whole army ate together.

Follows Jowett's a fortiori structure and states the premise that steel could not wound Ajax. Plato presupposes it ('than Ajax was invulnerable to steel'), and BEFORE's comparative left it implicit for a listener. Naming Socrates keeps 'him' from being read as Ajax, and the next clause's 'capturing him' then refers cleanly to Socrates. Reads well.

Checked element by element; nothing is dropped. It keeps the frost; the tremendous winter; the others staying indoors, or going out heavily clothed, shod, and with their feet wrapped in felt and fleeces; Socrates marching better, barefoot and in ordinary clothes; and the soldiers' resentment. 'Thinking he was looking down on them' renders Jowett's 'because he seemed to despise them' as the soldiers' perception, as in Plato's hos kataphronounta. It is now two clear sentences aloud, with spaced dashes, and the quote is correctly left open for 8.33.

Correct under the conventions. 8.33 is open. 8.34 reopens Alcibiades' speech with a single quote, nests Homer's line (Odyssey 4.242) in double quotes, and leaves the single quote open. 8.35 reopens it. The stated reason 'left open as at 8.11' is inaccurate, though. 8.11 currently closes its single quote after the double quote, even though its sentence runs on into 8.12, so the two parallel one-line verse paragraphs now differ. 8.34 is the one that follows the rule (see paragraph_problems, 8.11).
The reopening quote is required, because 8.35 continues Alcibiades' speech, which runs from 8.22 to 8.38. Lowercase 'while' correctly carries on Jowett's sentence across the verse line.

Plato's word is hubristou, the same root as 8.23's 'you are insolent' (hubristes). 'Insolent' restores that echo and drops the modern sexual or gratuitous slant of 'wanton'. Choosing it within Jowett's 'wanton', which in his usage also meant unruly and insolent, is a sound use of the Greek. No other translation is imported.

Restores Socrates as the agent, as in Jowett's 'making them pay their addresses to him' (in Plato he sets himself up as the beloved instead of the lover). No coercion is added beyond Jowett's 'making'. The parallel 'courting them ... court him' is clear aloud.
Faithful. 'I suspect' fits 'I am disposed to think' (tekmairomai), and 'come' is idiomatic for movement toward the person addressed. It sets up Socrates' 'come here' in 8.41.

Accurate against 8.43 and Plato. In the reclining order, 'below' (hypokato) means the next place, and speeches pass to the right. At 223a Socrates says 'if Agathon reclines below you', meaning between Alcibiades and himself, so 'below me' does mean 'on my right'. The gloss makes 8.43's 'praise his neighbor on the right', Alcibiades' 'between us' (8.42) and Socrates' objection readable. Dropping Jowett's 'on the couch', which is not in the Greek, removes the image of a lower couch. Minor: 'lie below me' on its own could suggest a stray innuendo, but the appositive follows at once.
'Oh no' works as comic exasperation for 'Alas' (Plato: o Zeu), and 'I beg you, let' is natural. The line stays drunk and funny.
'Hooray' and the active 'so that Socrates can praise me' keep Agathon's eager vanity and the joke. Faithful.
Jowett has 'the fair' (Plato: ton kalon). This matches 8.26 exactly and follows the glossary.
Restores Jowett's 'large quantities'. Plato's pampolun would allow the stronger word, but Jowett is the baseline, and the change is harmless.

paragraph_problems.issue: Glossary outlier, now conspicuous. Jowett's 'this fairest and wisest of men' (Agathon) is still rendered 'the handsomest and wisest of men'. R2-75/76/77/85 made every other 'fair' of persons in chapter 8 'beautiful', including 8.3's 'the most beautiful person here' for the same man and the same Greek word (kallistos). Suggested fix: 'crown the head of the most beautiful and wisest of men'. Low severity; not caused by R2-144/145, which are fine.

R2-158 introduced 'wits' end', but 8.31 keeps 'wit's end' for the same phrase in the same speech. The R2-158 revision resolves this by using 'wit's end'. If that revision is not taken, align 8.31 instead.

Outside this packet; a consistency follow-up to R2-82. 8.11 reads '"The wise physician skilled our wounds to heal"' and so closes its single quote, although Alcibiades' sentence continues into 8.12, which reopens it. After R2-82, the parallel one-line Homer paragraph at 8.34 correctly leaves the single quote open. To follow the multi-paragraph speech convention, 8.11 should drop its final single quote. Low severity; the editor's call if 8.11 is protected.

Optional. After R2-157, 'the statesman Pericles' is glossed at both 8.24 and 8.37. This is harmless, and the gloss at 8.37 helps the comparison with Nestor and Antenor, but 8.37 could be shortened to 'were like Pericles'.

summary: SRC4, chapter 8 (30 paragraphs, 35 edits): 33 accept, 2 revise, 0 reject. Every AFTER paragraph was read in full and checked against Jowett, and against Plato's Greek where a choice turned on it. No edit imports a reading from another translation, and no convention breaks were found (straight quotes, balanced multi-paragraph speech quotes, spaced em dashes, no ellipses, American spelling). The glosses are accurate and add no motive: Alcibiades as 'the famous Athenian politician and general', 'in the theater' (matches 1.34), the musician Olympus, and the statesman Pericles. The 'beautiful' changes (8.3, 8.4, 8.27, 8.45) agree with 8.26 and the glossary. 'Below me, in the place on my right' is correct against 8.43 and Plato's seating language. The Ajax a fortiori, 'making them court him' and 'lovers who have ever courted me' are faithful and frank, and the 8.33-8.35 quote structure now follows the convention. The banter at 8.6 and 8.40-8.44 stays drunk, candid and funny. Revisions: R2-149 restores Eryximachus's pompous 'passed a resolution', which echoes the 'motion' and 'vote' of chapter 1. R2-158 restores 'confessed', which echoes 8.24, and uses 'wit's end' to match 8.31. Follow-ups: 8.0's 'handsomest' is the last non-glossary 'fair'; 8.11 closes its quote where 8.34 now correctly leaves it open; the double Pericles gloss (8.24, 8.37) could optionally be trimmed.
